The Python part of the deck (slides 35–44), step by step: we start with loading and plotting the data and add one new thing per step, up to the 2019 forecast. The code is the code on the slides, character for character. Run the chunks in order. The short extras A to D after Step 10 repeat a few theory slides in Python; they are optional.

The data (`data/forecasting/aus_clothing_retail.csv`): the monthly turnover of clothing, footwear and personal accessory retailing in Australia, April 1982 to April 2019, with two columns, `month` (the first day of the month) and `value` (turnover in AUD million, not seasonally adjusted). Source: ABS, Retail Trade, Australia (8501.0), Table 11; CC BY 4.0.

## Step 1: Load and look

We read the file with polars and keep the ten years 2009–2018. The file sits in `sessions/01-foundations/`, so the path goes two folders up; `try_parse_dates=True` turns the month column into dates.

```{python}
import polars as pl
from plotnine import aes, geom_line, ggplot

# load the monthly sales and keep 2009-2018
file = "../../data/forecasting/aus_clothing_retail.csv"
df = pl.read_csv(file, try_parse_dates=True)
df = df.filter(
    pl.col("month").dt.year().is_between(2009, 2018))
print(df.head())

# plot the series
ggplot(df, aes("month", "value")) + geom_line()
```

Look first: sales grow, and every December has a peak that gets larger over the years (slide 25).

## Step 2: Split: fit and holdout

The rows are in time order, so the last 24 months (2017–2018) are the holdout: we fit on the past and test on the future. Never split a time series at random.

```{python}
# the sales as numbers, in time order
y = df["value"].to_numpy()

# fit on the first 96 months, hold out the last 24
train, test = y[:-24], y[-24:]
print(len(train), len(test))
```

96 months (2009–2016) to fit, 24 months (2017–2018) to test.

## Step 3: Naive and seasonal naive

The two simplest forecasts for the 24 holdout months. Naive repeats the last training month, December 2016; the seasonal naive repeats the last training year, 2016, twice.

```{python}
import numpy as np

# naive: repeat the last training month 24 times
naive = np.repeat(train[-1], 24)

# seasonal naive: repeat the last training year twice
snaive = np.resize(train[-12:], 24)
print(naive[:12])
print(snaive[:12])
```

Naive forecasts 3,330.5 AUD m, a Christmas, for every month; the seasonal naive forecasts January 2017 with January 2016 (1,875.7) and December with December (3,330.5).

## Step 4: How good? The MAE

The error is actual − forecast; the MAE is the mean of the errors without their signs (slide 22). One line per method.

```{python}
# MAE: the mean absolute error on the holdout
mae_snaive = np.mean(np.abs(test - snaive))
mae_naive = np.mean(np.abs(test - naive))
print(mae_snaive, mae_naive)
```

The seasonal naive misses by 67.2 AUD m a month on average, naive by 1,277.5: the December trap. On seasonal data the seasonal naive is the benchmark to beat (slide 30).

## Step 5: Smooth: a rolling average

A rolling average of 12 months holds every month of the year once, so the December peak cancels out and the trend is left (slide 26). `center=True` gives each month the average of the 12 months around it.

```{python}
# 12-month rolling average, centred: the trend
smooth = df.with_columns(
    trend=pl.col("value").rolling_mean(12, center=True))
print(smooth.drop_nulls())

# the sales and the trend in one chart
chart = ggplot(smooth, aes("month", "value")) + geom_line()
chart + geom_line(aes(y="trend"), color="blue")
```

The trend runs from 1,628.8 in July 2009 (the average month of 2009) to 2,089.8 in July 2018: flat to 2012, then growth. The first 6 and last 5 months have no value.

## Step 6: Exponential smoothing

Holt-Winters smooths a level, a trend and a season (slide 29). `seasonal="mul"` lets the December peak grow with the level; `seasonal_periods=12` says the data are monthly.

```{python}
import statsmodels.tsa.api as tsa

# Holt-Winters: a trend and a season that grows
hw = tsa.ExponentialSmoothing(
    train, trend="add", seasonal="mul",
    seasonal_periods=12,
    initialization_method="estimated").fit()
hw_fc = hw.forecast(24)
mae_hw = np.mean(np.abs(test - hw_fc))
print(mae_hw)
```

MAE 96.6: worse than the seasonal naive (67.2). A smarter method is not always a better forecast; test, do not assume.

## Step 7: Regression: trend and months

A regression on log sales with a trend `t` (1 to 120) and a dummy for each month `C(m)`, January as the baseline, as for the quarters of the chocolate shop (slide 19). `np.exp()` brings the forecast back from logs to AUD m.

```{python}
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

# t counts the months 1-120, m is the month 1-12
d = df.with_columns(
    t=pl.int_range(1, pl.len() + 1),
    m=pl.col("month").dt.month()).to_pandas()
# log sales on trend + month dummies, first 96 months
reg = smf.ols("np.log(value) ~ t + C(m)",
              data=d[:-24]).fit()
reg_fc = np.exp(reg.predict(d[-24:]))
mae_reg = np.mean(np.abs(test - reg_fc))
print(mae_reg)
```

MAE 54.5: the first method that beats the seasonal naive. `reg.summary()` shows the coefficients.

## Step 8: SARIMA

SARIMA works on log sales: it takes the change on last month and on the same month last year, and models how much of a surprise carries on (slide 29).

```{python}
# SARIMA on log sales: a change on last month
# and on last year, and the memory of surprises
sar = tsa.SARIMAX(
    np.log(train), order=(0, 1, 1),
    seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 12)).fit(disp=0)
sar_fc = np.exp(sar.forecast(24))
mae_sar = np.mean(np.abs(test - sar_fc))
print(mae_sar)
```

MAE 94.9: also worse than the seasonal naive on this holdout.

## Step 9: Compare the four

The four MAEs in one small table, written out by hand.

```{python}
# the four MAEs side by side
pl.DataFrame({
    "method": ["snaive", "hw", "reg", "sarima"],
    "MAE": [mae_snaive, mae_hw, mae_reg, mae_sar]})
```

The regression wins (54.5); the seasonal naive (67.2) comes second, ahead of SARIMA (94.9) and Holt-Winters (96.6). Slide 30 shows the same ranking with eleven methods.

## Step 10: Forecast 2019

Refit the winner on all 120 months and forecast the twelve months of 2019 (`t` 121 to 132). `obs_ci_lower` and `obs_ci_upper` are the 95 % band: it should hold the actual value in 95 of 100 months.

```{python}
# refit the winner on all 120 months
reg_all = smf.ols("np.log(value) ~ t + C(m)",
                  data=d).fit()

# 2019: t = 121 to 132, m = 1 to 12
new = pl.DataFrame({"t": range(121, 133),
                    "m": range(1, 13)}).to_pandas()

# the forecast and its 95 % band, back from logs
band = reg_all.get_prediction(new).summary_frame()
np.exp(band[["mean", "obs_ci_lower", "obs_ci_upper"]])
```

Plan December 2019 (row 11) with 3,430 AUD m; the band runs from 3,178 to 3,702 (slide 31). For stock, order towards the upper part of the band if a stock-out is expensive.

## Extra A: the two shops by hand

Optional: the hand examples of Part 2 (slides 12–19) in Python. The phone shop's contracts in weeks 1–8; `shift(1)` moves each value one week down, so the naive forecast of a week is the week before, and `rolling_mean(3).shift(1)` is the moving average of the 3 weeks before.

```{python}
# the phone shop: naive and moving average (3), week by week
hand = pl.read_csv("../../data/forecasting/hand_examples.csv")
phone = hand.filter(pl.col("example") == "contracts")
phone.with_columns(
    naive=pl.col("value").shift(1),
    ma3=pl.col("value").rolling_mean(3).shift(1))
```

Exponential smoothing with α 0.5, started at the first value (slide 15), and the trend line (slide 16):

```{python}
# exponential smoothing and the trend line
v = phone["value"].to_numpy()
ses = tsa.SimpleExpSmoothing(
    v, initialization_method="known", initial_level=v[0])
ses = ses.fit(smoothing_level=0.5, optimized=False)
print(ses.level, ses.forecast(1))
smf.ols("value ~ period", data=phone.to_pandas()).fit().params
```

The levels run from 40 to 52.25, the forecast of week 9. The trend line is 38.25 + 2 × week, so week 9 is 56.25.

The chocolate shop's quarters (slides 18 and 19): a regression on a trend and quarter dummies, Q1 as the baseline, forecasts year 4.

```{python}
# the chocolate shop: trend + quarter dummies, then year 4
shop = hand.filter(pl.col("example") == "webshop")
shop = shop.with_columns(quarter=(pl.col("period") - 1) % 4 + 1)
season = smf.ols("value ~ period + C(quarter)",
                 data=shop.to_pandas()).fit()
year4 = pl.DataFrame({"period": [13, 14, 15, 16],
                      "quarter": [1, 2, 3, 4]})
season.predict(year4.to_pandas())
```

Year 4: 32, 28, 31 and 43 (k EUR): 19 + 1 × 16 + 8 = 43 for the Christmas quarter.

## Extra B: stationary or not

Optional (slides 9 and 10). Noise is stationary; its running sum, a random walk, wanders off; the changes of the walk are the noise again, so differencing is the fix.

```{python}
# noise, a random walk and the changes of the walk
from plotnine import facet_wrap
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
noise = rng.normal(0, 1, 100)
walk = noise.cumsum()
changes = np.diff(walk, prepend=0)
sim = pl.DataFrame({"period": range(1, 101), "noise": noise,
                    "walk": walk, "changes": changes})
# one panel per series
long = sim.unpivot(index="period", variable_name="series")
chart = ggplot(long, aes("period", "value")) + geom_line()
chart + facet_wrap("series", ncol=1)
```

## Extra C: decomposition and the ADF test

Optional (slides 27 and 28). The seasonal index says how much a month sells against an average month; STL splits the series into trend, season and remainder.

```{python}
# the seasonal index of each month, January to December
index = tsa.seasonal_decompose(y, model="multiplicative", period=12)
print(index.seasonal[:12])

# STL: trend, season and remainder
stl = tsa.STL(y, period=12, robust=True).fit()
stl.plot()
```

December has an index of 1.59: it sells 59 % more than an average month. The ADF test asks whether a series wanders without a fixed mean; a small p (below 0.05) says stationary.

```{python}
# ADF p-values: levels, change on last month, change on last year
print("levels:", tsa.adfuller(y)[1])
print("change on last month:", tsa.adfuller(np.diff(y))[1])
print("change on last year:", tsa.adfuller(y[12:] - y[:-12])[1])
```

Sales in levels wander (p 0.99); both changes pass at 5 %.

## Extra D: errors that stick together

Optional (slides 31 and 32). The errors of the regression of Step 7 on the training months run in long waves: Durbin–Watson is 2 without autocorrelation and far below 2 when the errors stick together. SARIMA leaves almost none.

```{python}
# Durbin-Watson and lag-1 autocorrelation of the errors
from statsmodels.stats.stattools import durbin_watson
print("regression DW:", durbin_watson(reg.resid))
print("regression lag 1:", tsa.acf(reg.resid)[1])
print("SARIMA lag 1:", tsa.acf(sar.resid[13:])[1])
```

So the regression band of Step 10 is too narrow for later months. SARIMA, refitted on all 120 months, gives a band that widens with the horizon:

```{python}
# SARIMA on all 120 months: 2019 with its 95 % band
sar_all = tsa.SARIMAX(
    np.log(y), order=(0, 1, 1),
    seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 12)).fit(disp=0)
sar_band = sar_all.get_forecast(12).summary_frame()
np.exp(sar_band[["mean", "mean_ci_lower", "mean_ci_upper"]])
```

December 2019: 3,509 AUD m with a band from 3,227 to 3,816. The band is 209 AUD m wide in January and 589 in December; the regression's (Step 10) is 309 and 524.

## Appendix: open data for practice

Three open sources for your own forecasting practice (slide 50), none downloaded here; the textbook is Hyndman & Athanasopoulos (2021), *Forecasting: Principles and Practice*, 3rd ed., <https://otexts.com/fpp3> (Python edition <https://otexts.com/fpppy>).

- **ABS Retail Trade, Australia (8501.0)**: monthly turnover by state and industry, the source of our series; CC BY 4.0, <https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/industry/retail-and-wholesale-trade/retail-trade-australia>.
- **Eurostat**: monthly retail trade (`sts_trtu_m`) and nights at tourist accommodation (`tour_occ_nim`) by EU country; free reuse with the source acknowledged.
- **M5 competition data (Walmart)**: daily unit sales of 3,049 products in 10 US stores, 2011–2016; the competition terms apply.
